name: Bayes' Theorem
summary_definition: Bayes' theorem relates conditional probabilities: P(A|B) = P(B|A)·P(A) / P(B) — it tells you how to update the probability of a hypothesis given new evidence.
primary_explanation: The theorem states that the posterior probability of a hypothesis given evidence equals the likelihood of that evidence under the hypothesis, times the prior probability, divided by the total probability of the evidence. Its practical power comes from reversing conditionals: doctors know P(symptom|disease) but want P(disease|symptom), and spam filters know P(words|spam) but need P(spam|words). The prior matters most when evidence is weak or the hypothesis is rare — a rare disease with a good test can still have a low positive predictive value, because false positives from the healthy majority swamp true positives. Iterating Bayes' rule as data arrives is exactly what Bayesian learning does.

key_properties.value: Rare hypotheses stay improbable unless evidence is strong

applications: Medical testing: interpreting screening results for rare diseases.
Spam filtering and fraud detection: combining prior frequency with message evidence.
Machine learning: naive Bayes classifiers and Bayesian parameter estimation.

misconceptions.misconception_text: A 99% accurate test means a positive result is 99% likely to be correct.
misconceptions.correction_text: Positive predictive value depends on prevalence: with a 1-in-1000 disease, even a 99%-specific test yields mostly false positives among positives.
misconceptions.explanation: Bayes' theorem divides true positives by all positives — the healthy majority's false positives dominate when the base rate is low.

name: Central Limit Theorem
summary_definition: The central limit theorem states that the distribution of a sample mean approaches a normal distribution as sample size grows, regardless of the population's own distribution shape.
primary_explanation: Take repeated samples of size n from any finite-variance distribution — uniform, exponential, skewed, whatever — and average each. As n increases (rule of thumb 30+), those averages form an ever-tighter bell curve centered on the population mean with standard deviation σ/√n. This is why the normal distribution appears everywhere: it is the default shape of accumulated random variation, from measurement error to portfolio returns to election polls. It also gives the foundation for confidence intervals and hypothesis tests on means — z- and t-procedures assume normality of the estimator through this theorem, not of the raw data. The theorem fails for infinite-variance distributions such as the Cauchy, where averages never stabilize.

key_properties.value: Normal distribution of the sample mean
σ / √n — averages shrink variability by the square root of n
Independent observations, finite variance; population shape irrelevant

applications: Polling: margins of error computed from sample means.
Quality control: X-bar control charts detecting process drift.
Finance: approximating portfolio return distributions from many small bets.

misconceptions.misconception_text: The central limit theorem says any dataset becomes normal with enough data.
misconceptions.correction_text: It concerns the distribution of sample means/sums, not the raw observations themselves — individual data can stay heavily skewed forever.
misconceptions.explanation: The theorem normalizes an estimator formed by averaging, not the underlying variable being measured.

name: Normal Distribution
summary_definition: The normal (Gaussian) distribution is the symmetric bell-shaped probability density f(x) = (1/σ√(2π))·e^(-(x-μ)²/2σ²), fully determined by its mean μ and standard deviation σ.
primary_explanation: About 68% of draws fall within one σ of the mean, 95% within two, and 99.7% within three — the 68-95-99.7 rule. Its importance is both physical and mathematical: sums of many small independent effects produce normal variation (via the central limit theorem), and the distribution maximizes entropy for a fixed variance, making it the least-assumptive choice when only mean and spread are known. Natural quantities like heights, measurement errors, and noise often approximate it; returns in finance often do not, showing fat tails instead. The standardized form (μ=0, σ=1) gives z-scores, letting any normal variable be compared on one table — the backbone of classical inference.

key_properties.value: Mean μ (location) and standard deviation σ (scale)
Share of mass within 1σ, 2σ, 3σ of the mean
z = (x − μ)/σ maps any normal to the unit normal
All odd central moments are zero; kurtosis = 3 (excess kurtosis 0)

applications: Standardized testing and quality control (six sigma).
Statistical inference: z-tests, t-tests, and confidence intervals.
Noise modeling in signal processing and sensor fusion.

misconceptions.correction_text: Normality is a convenient approximation for averages of many small effects; counts, incomes, and financial returns are typically skewed or heavy-tailed.
misconceptions.explanation: The CLT produces normality of means, not of the raw variables themselves.

name: Law of Large Numbers
summary_definition: The law of large numbers states that the sample average converges to the true expected value as the number of independent trials grows — averages stabilize, even though individual outcomes never do.
primary_explanation: For independent identically distributed draws with finite mean μ, the sample mean X̄ₙ → μ almost surely as n → ∞ (strong law) or in probability (weak law). The practical meaning: short runs are noisy, long runs are fair — a coin 60% heads after 100 flips is unremarkable; after 100,000 flips the share will sit within a whisker of 50%. Convergence is slow: deviations shrink like 1/√n, so quadrupling precision requires quadrupling the data. The theorem requires finite mean — for heavy-tailed distributions like the Cauchy the sample mean wanders and never settles. Crucially, it says nothing about the next single outcome; it governs averages, not fortune.

key_properties.value: Deviation of the mean shrinks as σ/√n
Strong: converges almost surely; weak: in probability
Finite mean (and variance for rate statements)
Applies to averages, not individual future outcomes

applications: Casino and insurance mathematics: house edge materializes over volume.
A/B testing: stopping only when sample sizes make means reliable.
Monte Carlo simulation: estimates improve as runs accumulate.

misconceptions.misconception_text: After five heads in a row, tails is due (gambler's fallacy).
misconceptions.correction_text: Independent flips have no memory; the law of large numbers works by diluting streaks with future trials, not by balancing past ones.
misconceptions.explanation: The LLN constrains the long-run average and leaves every finite sequence, streaks included, fully possible.

name: Hypothesis Testing
summary_definition: Hypothesis testing is a procedure for deciding whether sample data contradicts a stated null hypothesis — it quantifies how surprising the observed result would be if the null were true.
primary_explanation: The method specifies a null hypothesis H₀ (usually 'no effect'), chooses a test statistic, computes a p-value — the probability of seeing data at least this extreme assuming H₀ — and rejects H₀ when the p-value falls below a preset α (commonly 0.05). Rejecting means the data are surprising under H₀, not that H₀ is false with 95% probability: the p-value is P(data|H₀), not P(H₀|data). Design choices matter as much as arithmetic: α sets the false-positive rate, sample size sets power (the chance of detecting a real effect), and multiple comparisons inflate false discoveries unless corrected. Preregistration of hypotheses and methods keeps the test honest.

key_properties.value: H₀: the default of no effect or no difference
Reject H₀ when p < α (α commonly 0.05)
Type I = false positive (α); Type II = false negative (β)
1 − β: probability of detecting a true effect

applications: Clinical trials: establishing whether a drug beats placebo.
A/B testing on product changes before full rollout.
Scientific replication: separating signal from noise in published findings.

misconceptions.misconception_text: p < 0.05 means there is a 95% probability the hypothesis is true.
misconceptions.correction_text: The p-value is P(data extreme | H₀ true) — it says nothing directly about the probability that the hypothesis holds.
misconceptions.explanation: Converting p-values to hypothesis probabilities requires Bayes' theorem with an explicit prior.

name: Markov Chains
summary_definition: A Markov chain is a random process where the next state depends only on the current state, not on the path taken — 'the future is independent of the past, given the present' — described by a transition matrix.
primary_explanation: States evolve by fixed transition probabilities: today's weather decides tomorrow's, regardless of last week's. Despite this memorylessness, chains exhibit rich long-run behavior: irreducible, aperiodic chains converge to a stationary distribution π satisfying πP = π, and the starting point is forgotten. Special structure gives more — reversible chains satisfy detailed balance, absorbing chains eventually trap in absorbing states with computable hitting probabilities, and finite chains are guaranteed to reach stationarity. Applications include Google's original PageRank (a random-surfer Markov chain), speech-recognition decoding, queueing models, and MCMC sampling, where designing a chain whose stationary distribution equals the target distribution makes hard integrals tractable.

key_properties.value: Transition matrix P with rows summing to 1
πP = π — reached by irreducible aperiodic chains

applications: PageRank: ranking web pages as a stationary distribution.
MCMC: sampling posteriors by simulating a chain (Metropolis-Hastings, Gibbs).
Reliability: modeling component lifecycles and equipment degradation.

misconceptions.misconception_text: Markov means the process has no randomness.
misconceptions.correction_text: Transitions are random — memorylessness only restricts dependence to the current state, not the outcome itself.
misconceptions.explanation: The chain is stochastic at every step; the constraint is on what information the next step conditions on.

name: Monte Carlo Method
summary_definition: Monte Carlo methods estimate quantities by drawing random samples and averaging the results — replacing hard closed-form calculations with repeated random experiment.
primary_explanation: If you cannot integrate a function analytically, sample points where it applies and average: the sample mean estimates the integral, with error shrinking as 1/√n. The name comes from Las Vegas casinos — the logic is the law of large numbers turned into a computational tool. Variants are everywhere: estimating π by throwing darts at a square, pricing options by simulating thousands of price paths, sizing risk by resampling portfolio returns (bootstrap), integrating posterior distributions in Bayesian models (MCMC), and rendering images by tracing light paths. Convergence is reliable but slow (sqrt rule), so variance-reduction tricks — importance sampling, antithetic variates, control variates — are used when precision is expensive.

key_properties.value: Random sampling + averaging to estimate integrals or probabilities
Works in high dimensions where grids become infeasible
Includes MCMC, bootstrap, option-pricing simulation, ray tracing

applications: Finance: option pricing and value-at-risk via simulated paths.
Physics: radiation transport and molecular dynamics sampling.
Engineering: reliability and tolerance analysis with random inputs.

misconceptions.misconception_text: Monte Carlo results depend on luck and are unreliable.
misconceptions.correction_text: Estimates vary run to run but converge at the known 1/√n rate; confidence bounds can be computed from the sample variance.
misconceptions.explanation: Randomness controls the error distribution precisely — that is what makes the method rigorous rather than lucky.

name: Correlation vs Causation
summary_definition: Correlation measures how two variables move together; causation means changing one changes the other. Association alone cannot distinguish cause from confounding, reverse direction, or coincidence.
primary_explanation: Ice-cream sales and drowning deaths correlate because heat drives both — the classic confounder. Three mechanisms produce correlation without the causal link one imagines: a hidden common cause (confounding), reversed direction (drowning doesn't sell ice cream, but the logic works backwards elsewhere), and pure chance in noisy data. Establishing causation requires design: randomized controlled trials break confounding by balancing groups on average; when randomization is impossible, natural experiments, instrumental variables, diff-in-diff designs, and explicit causal graphs approximate it. Granger causality in time series shows only predictive precedence. The discipline matters because interventions based on spurious correlation waste resources or cause harm.

key_properties.value: Asymmetric: intervention on cause changes effect
Common causes inflate or fabricate association

applications: Epidemiology: moving from observational signals to trial-confirmed risk factors.
Product analytics: separating feature engagement from retention drivers.
Policy evaluation: difference-in-differences around regulation changes.

misconceptions.misconception_text: A strong correlation implies one variable causes the other.
misconceptions.correction_text: Even r ≈ 1 can arise from a third variable or reverse causation; correlation constrains association, not mechanism.
misconceptions.explanation: Causal claims need a mechanism plus design (ideally randomization) that excludes common causes.

name: Maximum Likelihood
summary_definition: Maximum likelihood estimation chooses the parameter value under which the observed data would have been most probable — maximizing the likelihood function L(θ) = P(data|θ).
primary_explanation: Fix the data, treat θ as the free variable, and ask which θ makes the observed outcomes most likely. For i.i.d. samples the likelihood factorizes into a product of densities; maximizing it usually means maximizing its log, turning products into sums and derivatives into solvable equations. Fitting a Gaussian to data yields sample mean and variance; fitting logistic regression finds weights maximizing the probability of observed labels. MLE has strong properties: consistent, and asymptotically normal with the Cramér–Rao minimum variance at the efficient bound. It can overfit with little data — regularization (MAP estimation) or bias corrections address that. Bayes estimation extends it by weighting the likelihood with a prior.

key_properties.value: Maximize the log-likelihood (sum of log densities)
Consistent and asymptotically efficient under standard conditions
Biased or degenerate with tiny samples — hence MAP/regularization

applications: Fitting distributions: Gaussian, Poisson, and exponential parameters from data.
Machine learning: logistic regression and many neural losses are likelihoods.
Signal processing: estimating channel parameters from received symbols.

misconceptions.misconception_text: Likelihood and probability are the same function.
misconceptions.correction_text: Probability P(data|θ) sums to 1 over data for fixed θ; likelihood P(data|θ) as a function of θ has no such normalization.
misconceptions.explanation: Same numbers, different variable role — probability varies over outcomes, likelihood varies over parameters.

name: Probability Density Function
summary_definition: A probability density function f(x) describes the relative likelihood of a continuous random variable: probability over an interval is the area under f between its endpoints — individual points have probability zero.
primary_explanation: For continuous variables, the PDF is not a probability but a density: f(x) can exceed 1 (as long as total area is 1) and P(X = x) = 0 for every exact point — only intervals carry mass, computed as the integral of f. Two conditions define a valid density: nonnegative everywhere and integrating to one over the support. The cumulative distribution function F(x) = ∫₋∞ˣ f(t)dt is the running area, with f = F′ where smooth. Densities compose: multiplying independent densities gives the joint; integrating one variable out gives the marginal; normalizing a product gives the conditional — the three operations behind all multivariate modeling. The continuous analogue of a PMF, its role in inference is identical: the full description of uncertainty.

key_properties.value: P(X = x) = 0 — density is not probability

applications: Statistical modeling: specifying likelihoods for observed data.
Risk analysis: computing tail probabilities as tail areas of the density.
Signal processing: modeling noise distributions for detection thresholds.

misconceptions.misconception_text: A PDF value can be read directly as a probability.
misconceptions.correction_text: The PDF value is a density; probability comes from integrating it over an interval, so f(x) > 1 is perfectly legal.
misconceptions.explanation: Units of density are 'probability per unit x' — probabilities appear only after multiplying by a width.

name: Conditional Expectation
summary_definition: Conditional expectation E[Y|X] is the average value of Y once X is known — a function of X that gives the best single-number prediction of Y for each value of the conditioning variable.
primary_explanation: Unconditional expectation averages over everything; conditional expectation averages only over the uncertainty that remains after observing X. E[Y|X = x] is what you would bet on Y given that specific x — for joint normal variables it is linear in x, which is exactly why linear regression estimates the conditional mean. Iterated expectations, E[Y] = E[E[Y|X]], show the total average decomposes over layers of information, and conditioning reduces variance: Var(Y) = Var(E[Y|X]) + E[Var(Y|X)], the basis of analysis of variance. Martingale theory generalizes the idea: a process is a martingale when its next conditional expectation equals its current value — no predictable drift.

key_properties.value: E[Y|X] — expectation computed with X held fixed
Minimizes mean squared error among functions of X

applications: Regression: the true regression function is E[Y|X].
Finance: martingale pricing — discounted prices are martingales under risk-neutral measure.
Information: foundation for conditional mutual information and filtering.

misconceptions.misconception_text: E[Y|X = x] is a probability, not an expectation.
misconceptions.correction_text: It is a long-run average of Y values at that x — it can even take values Y itself never attains.
misconceptions.explanation: The conditional expectation is a summary of the conditional distribution, which may be spread widely around it.

name: Confidence Intervals
summary_definition: A confidence interval is a range built from sample data that captures the true parameter at a stated rate (e.g., 95%) across repeated sampling — point estimates plus a measure of their precision.
primary_explanation: The recipe: estimate ± (critical value × standard error). For a mean, x̄ ± 1.96·σ/√n gives a 95% interval when σ is known; with unknown σ and moderate n, the t-distribution widens it. The interpretation is procedural, not probabilistic-about-the-parameter: if you rebuilt the interval from 100 independent samples, about 95 of those intervals would contain the true μ — any single interval either does or doesn't, but you can't know which. Width shrinks with sample size (√n) and with variability, which is why bigger, cleaner experiments produce sharper estimates. Overlapping intervals between groups do not by themselves imply 'no significant difference' — the formal test compares the difference directly.

key_properties.value: x̄ ± 1.96 · σ/√n for means with known σ
95% of intervals from repeated samples capture the parameter
Shrinks with √n; grows with variability and confidence level

applications: Polling: reporting margin of error around vote shares.
Clinical trials: effect sizes reported with intervals, not just p-values.
Engineering tolerance: bounding measured means with stated coverage.

misconceptions.misconception_text: There is a 95% probability the true parameter lies in this specific interval.
misconceptions.correction_text: The parameter is fixed; it is the procedure that covers 95% of the time — this particular interval either contains it or not.
misconceptions.explanation: Frequentist intervals measure long-run procedure reliability, not parameter uncertainty for a realized interval.

name: Type I and II Errors
summary_definition: A Type I error rejects a true null hypothesis (false positive, rate α); a Type II error fails to reject a false null hypothesis (false negative, rate β). No test eliminates both — lowering one raises the other, given fixed data.
primary_explanation: Think courtroom: convicting an innocent person is Type I, letting a guilty person go free is Type II. In statistics, α is chosen in advance (0.05 conventional), while β depends on the true effect size, variability, and sample size — reducing β means running a bigger study (power = 1 − β). The trade-off curve is set by where you place the rejection threshold: move it to catch more true effects and you also catch more noise. Domain determines which error costs more: screening a lethal disease favors minimizing β (missed cases), while punishing fraud charges favors minimizing α (false accusations). The false-discovery rate extends this logic to hundreds of simultaneous tests.

key_properties.value: False positive — rejecting a true H₀
False negative — retaining a false H₀
1 − β; grows with effect size, variance reduction, and n
For fixed data, α and β move in opposite directions

applications: Medical screening: tolerating false positives to avoid missed diagnoses.
Quality inspection: balancing defective shipped vs good units discarded.
Security systems: tuning intrusion alarms to control false-alarm load.

misconceptions.misconception_text: A better test can eliminate both error types.
misconceptions.correction_text: With fixed data, the errors trade off; only more data or lower noise shifts the frontier and reduces both.
misconceptions.explanation: Sample size moves the whole ROC curve — threshold tweaks only move along it.

name: Linear Regression Fit
summary_definition: Linear regression fits the line ŷ = β₀ + β₁x that minimizes the squared vertical distances (residuals) between observed points and the fitted line, estimating how the outcome changes with the predictor.
primary_explanation: Ordinary least squares chooses coefficients that minimize Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)², producing the best linear unbiased estimate under classic assumptions: linear relationship, independent errors, constant variance, and no perfect collinearity. β₁ reads as the expected change in y for a one-unit rise in x, with a standard error and t-statistic attached; R² reports the share of outcome variance the model explains. Diagnostics matter more than the formula: residual plots reveal nonlinearity and heteroskedasticity, and omitted variables bias β₁ when a confounder correlates with both x and y. With one predictor the fit is a line; with many, it becomes a hyperplane — the same least-squares machinery.

key_properties.value: Ordinary least squares: minimize sum of squared residuals
β₁ = expected Δy per unit Δx, holding other predictors fixed
R² = share of variance explained (1 − SSE/SST)
Linearity, independent homoskedastic errors, no severe multicollinearity

applications: Forecasting: sales vs advertising spend, temperature vs energy use.
Economics: estimating returns to education controlling for experience.
Engineering: calibrating sensor output against reference measurements.

misconceptions.misconception_text: A high R² means the model identifies a causal relationship.
misconceptions.correction_text: R² measures fit, not causality — confounded or overfitted models can score high while implying nothing about interventions.
misconceptions.explanation: Fit statistics describe in-sample association; causal identification comes from design or assumptions outside the regression.

name: Newton's Second Law F=ma
summary_definition: Newton's second law states that the net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration: F = ma — force is the rate of change of momentum, and acceleration follows the unbalanced force.
primary_explanation: The law converts dynamics into bookkeeping: sum every force vector acting on a body, and the resultant sets the acceleration, a = F_net/m. The same 10 N shove accelerates a toy car ten times harder than a heavy cart — inertia (mass) resists change of motion. In its fuller form, F = dp/dt, it also covers variable-mass systems like rockets ejecting propellant, where thrust arises from momentum carried away. Force and acceleration are vectors, so components are solved independently on chosen axes, which is why projectile motion splits into a horizontal constant-velocity part and a vertical constant-acceleration part. The law is exact in inertial frames and only apparent (via fictitious forces) in accelerating ones.

key_properties.value: Inertia: larger m requires more force for the same a
Inertial reference frames; near-relativistic speeds use F = γ³ma

applications: Vehicle design: braking distances and crumple zones from deceleration forces.
Rocketry: thrust from expelled momentum (variable-mass form).
Structural engineering: load paths computed as ma responses.

misconceptions.misconception_text: An object moving at constant speed has no forces acting on it.
misconceptions.correction_text: Zero net force means zero acceleration, not zero motion — constant-velocity motion needs balanced forces (e.g., engine thrust equals friction).
misconceptions.explanation: F=ma links force to change in velocity; steady velocity is perfectly compatible with nonzero individual forces that cancel.

name: Conservation of Momentum
summary_definition: The total momentum of a closed system stays constant when no external force acts: m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ before equals m₁v₁' + m₂v₂' after — momentum is never created or destroyed, only transferred.
primary_explanation: Because F = dp/dt, zero net external force means total momentum p is constant — a conservation law valid in all inertial frames regardless of whether collisions are elastic or sticky. Two ice skaters pushing apart, a rifle's recoil, and a rocket's exhaust all follow the same accounting: the system's center of mass keeps moving as it always did while internal parts redistribute motion. In collisions, pairing momentum conservation with kinetic-energy accounting classifies outcomes: elastic collisions conserve both (billiard balls approximately), inelastic ones conserve momentum but lose kinetic energy to heat and deformation, and perfectly inelastic ones stick together. Momentum is a vector — directions must be handled component by component.

key_properties.value: Holds for elastic and inelastic interactions alike
Unforced system's center of mass moves uniformly

applications: Collision reconstruction: deriving speeds from debris and skid marks.
Rocket propulsion: exhaust momentum balances vehicle momentum gain.
Particle physics: inferring unseen particles from missing momentum.

misconceptions.misconception_text: Kinetic energy is always conserved in collisions.
misconceptions.correction_text: Momentum is always conserved in closed systems; kinetic energy only survives elastic collisions — most real collisions lose some to heat, sound, and deformation.
misconceptions.explanation: The two conservation statements answer different questions; only momentum has the universal condition (no external force).

records.title: Definition of Conservation of Momentum
records.content: The total momentum of a closed system stays constant when no external force acts: m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ before equals m₁v₁' + m₂v₂' after — momentum is never created or destroyed, only transferred.

chunks.text_content: Conservation of Momentum: The total momentum of a closed system stays constant when no external force acts: m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ before equals m₁v₁' + m₂v₂' after — momentum is never created or destroyed, only transferred.

Because F = dp/dt, zero net external force means total momentum p is constant — a conservation law valid in all inertial frames regardless of whether collisions are elastic or sticky. Two ice skaters pushing apart, a rifle's recoil, and a rocket's exhaust all follow the same accounting: the system's center of mass keeps moving as it always did while internal parts redistribute motion. In collisions, pairing momentum conservation with kinetic-energy accounting classifies outcomes: elastic collisions conserve both (billiard balls approximately), inelastic ones conserve momentum but lose kinetic energy to heat and deformation, and perfectly inelastic ones stick together. Momentum is a vector — directions must be handled component by component.

Key properties and applications of Conservation of Momentum: Condition: No net external force (closed system). Form: Σmᵢvᵢ = constant, component-wise. Independence: Holds for elastic and inelastic interactions alike. Center-of-mass link: Unforced system's center of mass moves uniformly. Applications: Collision reconstruction: deriving speeds from debris and skid marks. Rocket propulsion: exhaust momentum balances vehicle momentum gain. Particle physics: inferring unseen particles from missing momentum.

Common misconception about Conservation of Momentum: Kinetic energy is always conserved in collisions. Correction: Momentum is always conserved in closed systems; kinetic energy only survives elastic collisions — most real collisions lose some to heat, sound, and deformation.

name: Work-Energy Theorem
summary_definition: The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: W_net = ΔKE = ½mv² − ½mu² — force applied over distance is exactly what changes speed.
primary_explanation: Integrating F = ma along the path gives the theorem: every joule of net work done on a body shows up as kinetic energy. A car braking from 100 km/h to 50 dissipates three quarters of its KE through friction's negative work; a crane lifting a beam at constant speed does positive work against gravity that becomes gravitational potential energy rather than KE — which is why the theorem is usually generalized into energy conservation by including potential terms. Work is a scalar built from a vector product (W = F·d·cosθ), so forces perpendicular to motion — like gravity on a horizontal roll — do zero work. The approach bypasses acceleration details: with forces known as functions of position, energy methods yield speeds without solving the full trajectory.

key_properties.value: W = ∫F·ds — force component along the path
Positive work speeds up; negative work slows down
Only true for conservative forces; friction makes work path-dependent

applications: Braking systems: sizing friction materials for required energy dissipation.
Ballistic and impact testing: inferring speeds from deformation work.
Machine design: motor sizing from required kinetic-energy changes.

misconceptions.misconception_text: A force can do work without moving the point of application.
misconceptions.correction_text: Work requires displacement along the force — a stationary wall exerts force but does zero work.
misconceptions.explanation: W = F·d collapses to zero when d is zero, however large the force.

name: Angular Momentum Conservation
summary_definition: When net external torque is zero, a system's total angular momentum L = r × p (or Iω for rotation) stays constant — spinners speed up when they pull mass inward because L cannot change.
primary_explanation: Angular momentum is the rotational counterpart of linear momentum, and τ_net = dL/dt mirrors F = dp/dt: zero net torque freezes L. A pirouette drawing arms in reduces her moment of inertia I, so ω must rise to keep Iω constant — the same physics that makes ice skaters spin faster, planets swing faster at perihelion (Kepler's second law is angular-momentum conservation in gravity), and galaxies flatten into disks. Direction matters: L points along the spin axis by the right-hand rule, so gyroscopic devices resist changes to their orientation, producing precession instead. In collisions, angular momentum conservation supplements linear momentum when impacts occur off-center, determining post-collision rotation.

key_properties.value: L = r × p; for rigid bodies L = Iω

applications: Gyroscopes and navigation: attitude control in aircraft and spacecraft.
Planetary motion: perihelion speed-up from conserved L.
Sports science: dive and ski-jump tucks trading L for rotation rate.

misconceptions.misconception_text: Pulling mass inward creates angular momentum out of nothing.
misconceptions.correction_text: L = Iω is fixed when torque is zero — decreasing I necessarily increases ω; the angular momentum was there all along.
misconceptions.explanation: Only the distribution of existing L among parts of the system changes, never the total.

name: Torque and Lever Arms
summary_definition: Torque is the rotational effect of a force: τ = r × F, magnitude rF·sinθ — it depends on how far the force acts from the pivot and on its angle, not on force alone.
primary_explanation: Where F = ma governs straight-line motion, τ = Iα governs spinning: torque plays the role of force, moment of inertia I the role of mass, and angular acceleration α that of a. The lever arm (moment arm) is the perpendicular distance from pivot to the force's line of action — push a door at the hinge and the lever arm is zero, however hard you push. Loosening a stubborn bolt with a longer wrench raises r and multiplies torque; a force at 90° contributes fully, one pulling parallel to r contributes nothing (sinθ factor). Statics is the special case Στ = 0, the condition balancing seesaws, bridge trusses, and crane booms, while net torque driving rotation couples with angular momentum through τ = dL/dt.
applications: Wrench and tool design: multiplying manual force through length.
Crane and bridge engineering: moment balance about support points.
Biomechanics: joint moments from muscle forces and moment arms.

misconceptions.misconception_text: Bigger force always means more turning effect.
misconceptions.correction_text: Turning effect also depends on lever arm and angle — a large force through the pivot produces zero torque.
misconceptions.explanation: Torque is the cross product r × F; geometry can nullify even a huge force.

name: Center of Mass Calculation
summary_definition: The center of mass is the mass-weighted average position r_cm = Σmᵢrᵢ/Σmᵢ — the single point where an object's mass can be treated as concentrated for translational motion and gravity torque accounting.
primary_explanation: For a system of particles, the center of mass is the weighted mean of positions, weighting each by its mass; for continuous bodies the sum becomes an integral ∫r dm. It has two powers: (1) external forces accelerate the center of mass exactly as if all mass were there — a thrown wrench's CM traces a perfect parabola while the tool tumbles; and (2) gravity's torque on a rigid body equals the weight acting at the CM, which is why 'hanging from the CM' is stable and support must straddle the CM for balance. Symmetric objects place it at the geometric centroid (uniform sphere, rod midpoint); irregular or hollow shapes need the integral, and the CM can lie outside the material entirely — a banana's or boomerang's CM is in the air beside it.

key_properties.value: External forces move the CM as if all mass were concentrated there
Hollow or extended bodies may exclude their CM from material

applications: Vehicle stability: keeping the CM low and within the wheelbase.
Robotics and aerospace: fuel slosh and attitude control about the CM.
Structural engineering: load balance and overturning-moment checks.

misconceptions.misconception_text: The center of mass must be located inside the object.
misconceptions.correction_text: It is a mathematical average position — for hollow, arch, or boomerang shapes it can lie in empty space outside the material.
misconceptions.explanation: Averaging positions weighted by mass needs no matter at the average point itself.

name: Simple Harmonic Motion Oscillator
summary_definition: A simple harmonic oscillator moves under a restoring force proportional to displacement (F = −kx), producing sinusoidal motion at angular frequency ω = √(k/m) with period T = 2π√(m/k).
primary_explanation: The defining feature is linearity of the restoring force: double the stretch, double the pull-back. Solving F = −kx = ma yields x(t) = A·cos(ωt + φ), an endlessly repeating sine wave whose frequency depends only on stiffness and mass — not on amplitude, the remarkable isochronism that makes pendulum clocks work. Energy sloshes between potential (½kx², maximal at the turning points) and kinetic (½mv², maximal at the center) while their sum stays fixed. Damping (friction, air resistance) adds a decaying envelope and drives the system to rest, while an external periodic force near resonance makes amplitude grow — the behavior exploited in radios, tuning forks, and seismometers, and feared in bridges and buildings.

key_properties.value: E = ½kA² constant; exchanges KE ↔ PE twice per cycle

applications: Timekeeping: pendulum and balance-wheel oscillators.
Filters and receivers: RLC circuits are electrical SHM tuned to frequencies.
Seismology and vibration testing: modeling building response to quakes.

misconceptions.misconception_text: A stiffer spring makes the oscillator slower.
misconceptions.correction_text: T = 2π√(m/k): stiffer springs raise k and shorten the period — the oscillator speeds up.
misconceptions.explanation: Frequency grows with stiffness and shrinks with mass; spring stiffness and inertia pull frequency in opposite directions.

name: Hooke's Law Springs
summary_definition: Hooke's law: a spring's restoring force is proportional to its extension, F = −kx — twice the stretch, twice the pull-back, with stiffness k setting the proportionality.
primary_explanation: For deformations within the elastic limit, springs obey F = −kx, the minus sign marking a force that always points toward equilibrium. The constant k is the spring's stiffness (N/m): a 100 N/m spring stretched 5 cm pulls back 5 N. The stored potential energy ½kx² grows quadratically with stretch, which is the energy budget cushions, trampolines, and suspension systems meter out. Hooke's law is a small-deformation approximation — stretch far enough and the force sublinearizes until the spring yields or breaks, the tensile counterpart of plastic flow. As the linear restoring law behind SHM (ω = √(k/m)) and the model for atomic bonds vibrating about their equilibrium, it underlies both engineering springs and the thermal physics of solids.

key_properties.value: U = ½kx² — area under the F-x triangle
Linear elastic regime only; beyond it, anharmonic then plastic

applications: Vehicle suspension: spring rate tuning for load and comfort.
Seismometers: inertial mass on a spring converting ground motion to readable displacement.
Materials testing: stiffness measurements from force-extension curves.

misconceptions.misconception_text: Hooke's law holds for any stretch, however large.
misconceptions.correction_text: It is a small-deformation approximation; past the proportional limit the F-x curve bends and the spring permanently deforms or breaks.
misconceptions.explanation: Real materials transition linear-elastic → anharmonic → plastic, so k itself drifts at large strains.

name: Friction Static and Kinetic
summary_definition: Static friction resists the start of motion up to μₛN, while kinetic friction acts during sliding at the lower μₖN — roughly constant regardless of speed — so objects are hardest to start moving, easier to keep moving.
primary_explanation: Friction is a contact force parallel to surfaces, arising from microscopic welding and deformation of asperities. Before anything moves, static friction takes whatever value is needed to cancel the applied force, up to its ceiling fₛ ≤ μₛN — beyond that the contact breaks loose and kinetic friction takes over at fₖ = μₖN, typically 20–80% smaller than the static peak. This drop explains the lurch when a stuck box finally breaks free, why anti-lock brakes keep tires in the static regime (higher force, steerable), and why a leaned-over bike tire grips: banking raises the normal force N. Kinetic friction is nearly speed-independent, so sliding deceleration a = μₖg depends only on the surfaces.

key_properties.value: fₛ ≤ μₛN — self-adjusting up to a maximum
μₛ > μₖ for typical surface pairs
Opposes relative sliding or its tendency

applications: Braking and tire design: keeping wheels in static (rolling) contact.
Civil engineering: base friction in foundations and slope stability.
Machinery: clutch and belt design from μₛ/μₖ specifications.

misconceptions.misconception_text: Kinetic friction increases with how fast you slide.
misconceptions.correction_text: The Coulomb model makes kinetic friction independent of sliding speed (and of contact area) — only normal force and surface pair matter.
misconceptions.explanation: Speed dependence appears only at extreme velocities where heating softens surfaces — outside the standard model.

name: Projectile Kinematics Trajectory
summary_definition: Projectile motion splits into independent uniform horizontal motion and constant-acceleration vertical motion (a = −g), tracing a parabola y = x·tanθ − gx²/(2v₀²cos²θ) under ideal no-drag conditions.
primary_explanation: Once launched, gravity is the only force (ignoring air), and vector independence lets each axis be solved alone: horizontal velocity v₀cosθ never changes, vertical velocity v₀sinθ − gt falls linearly, and combining x = v₀cosθ·t with the y-equation eliminates time to give the parabola. The launch angle that maximizes range on level ground is 45°, reduced for raised targets; time of flight depends only on the vertical component; and the apex occurs when the vertical velocity passes through zero. Range scales with v₀², explaining artillery tables. Air drag breaks the symmetry — real trajectories fall shorter on descent and peak slightly later — which is why ballistic coefficients exist, but the vacuum parabola remains the first-order model taught and used.

key_properties.value: x: constant velocity; y: constant acceleration −g
R = v₀² sin(2θ)/g, maximized at θ = 45°
t = 2v₀ sinθ / g for return to launch height

applications: Ballistics and artillery: firing tables from range equations.
Sports analytics: optimizing serve, shot-put, and free-kick angles.
Firefighting and rescue: aiming hose and throw trajectories.

misconceptions.misconception_text: At the top of its arc a projectile has zero velocity.
misconceptions.correction_text: Only the vertical component vanishes at the apex — the horizontal component persists, which is why the projectile keeps moving forward there.
misconceptions.explanation: Velocity is a vector; a zeroed component is not zero speed (except straight up-and-down launches).

name: Elastic vs Inelastic Collisions
summary_definition: Elastic collisions conserve both momentum and kinetic energy (balls, gas molecules); inelastic collisions conserve momentum but convert some KE to heat, sound, and deformation — perfectly inelastic ones end with the bodies stuck together.
primary_explanation: The classification hangs on energy bookkeeping, not on softness or noise. In one dimension an elastic collision between masses m₁ and m₂ swaps or shares velocities according to conservation of both p and KE — deriving the well-known 'equal masses exchange velocities' result. In the real world only approximately elastic encounters happen (billiard balls, neutron moderation); anything with crunch, splash, or heat is inelastic, and the perfectly inelastic case (sticking) loses the most KE allowed while still satisfying momentum conservation. The lost KE is exactly the energy that went into deformation and thermal motion — it never vanishes. Collisions off-center add rotational outcomes, requiring angular-momentum conservation alongside the linear equations.

key_properties.value: Conserved in both types (no external force)
e = separation speed / approach speed; e=1 elastic, e=0 perfectly inelastic

applications: Vehicle crash design: engineered crumpling maximizes KE absorption per occupant g-load.
Gas kinetics: elastic molecular collisions maintain temperature equilibrium.
Ballistics and sports: restitution coefficients for equipment standards.

misconceptions.misconception_text: Inelastic collisions violate conservation of energy.
misconceptions.correction_text: Total energy is conserved — kinetic energy merely transforms into heat, sound, and deformation; only KE (not energy) is lost.
misconceptions.explanation: The conservation law applies to the full energy budget, of which kinetic energy is just one transferable part.

name: Escape Velocity Formula
summary_definition: Escape velocity is the minimum launch speed needed to break free of a body's gravity forever without further thrust: v = √(2GM/r) — about 11.2 km/s from Earth's surface.
primary_explanation: Set the total energy (kinetic plus gravitational potential) to zero and solve: the kinetic energy ½mv² must exactly cancel the depth of the potential well −GMm/r, giving v = √(2GM/r). At that speed the object coasts uphill forever, slowing asymptotically toward zero but never falling back — below it, gravity eventually turns the trajectory around. The remarkable independence of mass appears because m cancels: a pebble and a spacecraft need the same speed from the same place. Escape velocity rises with the central mass and falls with distance (at twice the radius it is 1/√2 as large), which is why the Sun's 617 km/s makes Earth-bound launches harder than the Moon's 2.38 km/s makes lunar departures easy. Temperature-driven atmospheric loss follows the same logic via molecular speeds.

key_properties.value: Total energy ≥ 0 (KE cancels potential well depth)
Object mass cancels — same speed for all payloads

applications: Rocketry: computing minimum Δv budgets for orbit departure.
Planetary science: explaining atmospheric retention (light gases exceed v_esc thermally).
Astrophysics: black-hole escape speed reaches c at the event horizon.

misconceptions.misconception_text: Escape velocity means traveling fast enough to outrun gravity's pull continuously.
misconceptions.correction_text: The escaper keeps feeling gravity the whole way — it just never wins: with total energy ≥ 0 the trajectory is open (parabolic/hyperbolic) and distance grows without bound.
misconceptions.explanation: Gravity falls as 1/r²; once KE exceeds well depth, the object always retains some speed.

name: Kepler's First Law Ellipses
summary_definition: Kepler's first law: every planet moves on an ellipse with the Sun at one focus — orbits are not circles with the center at the Sun, and nothing sits at the geometric center.
primary_explanation: Observing Mars across oppositions, Kepler rejected the 2,000-year-old deferent circles and fitted an ellipse — Sun at one focus, the other focus empty. The orbit's shape is quantified by eccentricity e: 0 is a perfect circle, e between 0 and 1 an ellipse (Earth e ≈ 0.017, nearly circular; Mercury 0.206, visibly oval), and e ≥ 1 open parabolic/hyperbolic paths for one-time visitors like comets. Perihelion (closest) and aphelion (farthest) mark the extremes, at distances a(1−e) and a(1+e). The law emerges inevitably from an inverse-square central force — Newton derived the conic-section orbits from his law of gravitation, showing Kepler's empirical rule and F = GMm/r² are the same statement. Paired with the second law (equal areas in equal times), it fully fixes the planar motion.

key_properties.value: Ellipse with Sun at one focus
e = 0 circle; 0 < e < 1 ellipse; e ≥ 1 open orbit
Conic sections follow from inverse-square central forces

applications: Mission planning: Hohmann transfers between elliptical orbits.
Exoplanet characterization: radial-velocity curves reveal orbital eccentricity.
Comet prediction: distinguishing bound ellipses from parabolic flybys.

misconceptions.misconception_text: The Sun sits at the center of each planetary ellipse.
misconceptions.correction_text: The Sun occupies a focus, offset from the center by ae — the center is empty space, which is why Earth's distance from the Sun varies through the year.
misconceptions.explanation: A focus and an ellipse's center are distinct points; the offset equals eccentricity times semi-major axis.

summary_definition: A simple pendulum's period is T = 2π√(L/g) — set by string length and gravity alone, independent of mass and (for small swings) of amplitude.
primary_explanation: For small angles (under about 10–15°), sinθ ≈ θ turns the pendulum's equation of motion into the same linear restoring law as a spring, with effective k/m = g/L — hence the period T = 2π√(L/g). Galileo noticed the amplitude independence (isochronism) from church-lamp swings; it made pendulums the first precise timekeepers, with Huygens' clock exploiting it in 1656. Mass cancels, so a heavy and light bob on the same length swing in step; length tunes the rate (a 1 m pendulum has T ≈ 2 s, the basis of the seconds pendulum). Large swings lengthen the period — the nonlinearity that makes a grandfather clock's swing slow over weeks unless driven — and the same formula gives g from measured T and L, a classic gravimetry technique.

key_properties.value: Period unaffected by mass and (approximately) by amplitude
Measured T with known L yields g
Large swings lengthen T; formula becomes inaccurate beyond ~15°

applications: Timekeeping: grandfather and pendulum clocks tuned by bob position.
Gravimetry: measuring local g from swing period.
Seismology: historic tiltmeters and early inertial instruments.

misconceptions.misconception_text: A heavier bob makes the pendulum swing faster.
misconceptions.correction_text: Mass cancels from T = 2π√(L/g) — only length and gravity set the rate.
misconceptions.explanation: Both restoring force (mg sinθ) and inertia (m) scale with mass, so it divides out of the equation of motion.

name: Photosynthesis
summary_definition: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants, algae, and cyanobacteria capture light energy and convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen: 6CO2 + 6H2O + light → C6H12O6 + 6O2.
primary_explanation: The process runs in two connected stages inside the chloroplast. The light reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes: chlorophyll absorbs photons, water is split (photolysis) releasing the oxygen we breathe, and the energy drives production of ATP and NADPH. The Calvin cycle in the stroma then uses that ATP and NADPH to fix atmospheric CO2 into glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, the precursor to glucose and other organic molecules — the enzyme RuBisCO performs the critical carbon-fixing step. Overall efficiency is modest (1-2% of incident sunlight), yet photosynthesis underpins nearly every food chain and is responsible for the oxygenated atmosphere. It is also the target of research into artificial leaves and crop engineering to raise carbon fixation rates.

key_properties.value: Thylakoid membranes: photolysis of water, ATP + NADPH produced, O2 released
Stroma: CO2 fixed by RuBisCO into sugar using ATP and NADPH

applications: Agriculture: optimizing light, CO2, and water to raise crop yield.
Climate science: quantifying the ocean and land carbon sinks.
Biotechnology: engineering RuBisCO and C4 pathways for higher efficiency.

misconceptions.misconception_text: Plants only photosynthesize during the day and respire at night.
misconceptions.correction_text: Respiration runs continuously in all living cells; photosynthesis simply dominates during daylight, masking daytime respiration.
misconceptions.explanation: Daytime gas exchange shows net O2 release because photosynthetic O2 production exceeds respiratory consumption.
